content.$t:
Russia-Africa · Special Report

By William Aaron Turner, President of Infinitum Corporation · Russia-Africa section

I’m not a journalist. I’m a businessman. I’ve spent decades making money, not in newsrooms. So when I look at the third Russia-Africa Summit that just concluded in Moscow, I don’t see a geopolitical chess match. I see a trade fair. And from where I sit—with my firm doing work in Moscow and across multiple continents—the numbers tell a story that speaks for itself.

Let’s start with the scoreboard. Delegations from 48 of Africa’s 54 countries attended, with 22 represented by heads of state—up from 17 in 2023. The Kremlin says 33 intergovernmental, departmental, and commercial documents were scheduled for signing, and a new cooperation plan covering 2027 to 2029 was adopted. The event also produced a political declaration and a separate agreement on civilian applications of artificial intelligence.

That is not a photo op. That is a pipeline.

Russia-Africa trade exceeded $27 billion in 2025, compared with approximately $16.8 billion in 2019, when the first summit was held in Sochi. President Putin has set a target of $50 billion, and he told the summit plainly: “We are confident the current level of the Russian-African trade turnover, and it stands at $27 bln, is far from being the limit”. Russian agricultural exports to Africa increased 35 percent in value during the first half of 2026 to $2.9 billion, with wheat shipments reaching record levels.

Is $27 billion impressive compared to China’s $348 billion or the EU’s $395 billion? No. But trade is not a beauty contest. It is about what the capital actually does. And the trajectory matters.

I don’t care about the rhetoric. I care about what the capital actually does. The 15,000 sanctions have not worked. The scoreboard proves it.

The Food Security Guarantee

Let me put this in terms a businessman understands. More than 40 African countries receive Russian grain and fertilizer. In 2025, Russia shipped over 18 million tonnes of grain to Africa. In the first nine months of 2026 alone, another 13 million tonnes. Mineral fertilizer deliveries reached approximately 1.5 million tonnes last year and have already exceeded 2.2 million tonnes this year.

Putin called this “a concrete, tangible contribution to ensuring food security across the entire African continent”. Russia also annually allocates funds to the UN World Food Program for projects supporting African nations and regularly provides free humanitarian aid.

For a continent that imports a significant share of its wheat and fertilizer, this is not charity. It is supply-chain reliability. When other suppliers impose conditions, Russia delivers. That distinction matters to every purchasing manager and every finance minister on the continent.

Nuclear Energy: From Dialogue to Delivery

Rosatom is not selling press releases. It is building. The state nuclear corporation is constructing Egypt’s first nuclear power plant, El Dabaa—four 1,200-MW power units with Russian-designed VVER-1200 reactors. It will become only the second nuclear power station on the African continent, after South Africa’s Koeberg plant.

Rosatom CEO Alexei Likhachev told reporters at the summit that the company is in advanced discussions on floating nuclear power plant projects with Egypt, Togo, Namibia, and Tanzania. Deputy division head Vladimir Aptekarev noted that 38 of Africa’s more than 50 countries have sufficient coastline to host a Russian-made floating power unit, which can be towed to a destination, require less land infrastructure, and operate for up to 60 years under a power purchase agreement model.

On the sidelines of the summit, Rosatom signed a memorandum of understanding with Togo’s Ministry of Energy on peaceful nuclear cooperation.

Show me the Western company doing that in Africa right now. Show me the U.S. Export-Import Bank financing a nuclear plant in Togo. You can’t, because it isn’t happening. Russia walked in with a catalogue, a financing package, and a training pipeline. That is what a real partner looks like.

Security Cooperation: Stability as a Precondition for Investment

I would be a bad businessman if I pretended that security does not matter to investment. It matters more than anything. You cannot build a mine, a factory, or a logistics corridor if the government cannot control the roads.

Russia has intergovernmental agreements on military and military-technical cooperation with 45 African countries. African servicemen and law enforcement officers are being trained at Russian educational institutions. Russia is helping African states “maintain internal stability and security and strengthen their defense capabilities,” Putin said.

The Africa Corps, which is directly under the control of Russia’s defense ministry, provides combat support and military training. In Niger, when mutinous soldiers seized Air Base 101 at Diori Hamani International Airport in August 2026, Africa Corps personnel helped Nigerien loyalist forces regain control. Russia’s ambassador to Niger, Viktor Voropaev, publicly acknowledged the intervention, saying Russian forces had helped “repress a mutiny”. BBC analysts noted that Russia is “increasingly demonstrating that it can provide something perhaps even more valuable to the military rulers of Niger, Mali and Burkina Faso: protection for the governments themselves”.

This is a security-for-sovereignty arrangement. African governments invite Russian instructors because they want to defend their own territory. For a businessman, this is the foundation. Security enables investment. Investment enables growth. Growth enables prosperity. Russia is providing the first link in that chain.

The Historical Foundation: A Track Record That Cannot Be Erased

Let’s get one thing straight, because Western commentary on Russia in Africa is usually a mix of amnesia and projection. Russia never colonized a single square mile of Africa. It never participated in the transatlantic slave trade.

Even Foreign Policy magazine—hardly a Kremlin mouthpiece—acknowledged the substance of this history. The Russian Embassy in South Africa stated plainly: “Russia was among the few world powers that neither had colonies in Africa or elsewhere nor participated in [the] slave trade throughout its history. Russia helped, in every possible way, the peoples of the African continent to attain their freedom and sovereignty”.

During the Nigerian Civil War, the Soviet Union supported the Federal Government in Lagos from the onset of the conflict, while the United States and Britain largely stood aside. That is the memory African leaders carry into the room. It is not sentimentality. It is a track record. And in business, track records matter more than press clippings.

The Summit’s Broader Commitments

The summit was not just about trade and security. On education, Putin announced that nearly 40,000 African students are currently studying at Russian universities, and Russia will increase university quotas for African students, including state-funded places. On healthcare, Russia is expanding pharmaceutical supplies and mobile laboratories.

These are not abstract promises. They are institutional commitments with timelines and budgets attached.

The Ukraine War’s African Testing Ground

The war in Ukraine is not just a European conflict. It is being tested and exported to Africa.

CNN reported in September 2026 that roughly 15 Ukrainian drone specialists have been deployed to northern Mali to assist local rebel forces fighting Russian troops. A Ukrainian Defense Intelligence source told CNN that several Ukrainian specialists were also stationed in Sudan, and that troops from Chad, Niger, and Burkina Faso had traveled to Mali to receive drone training from Ukrainian soldiers. The desert heat, the dust, the vast distances—these are testing grounds. The lessons learned are being fed back into the war against Russia.

Russia is doing the same with Africa Corps. The tactics being refined in the Sahel are the same tactics being used in Ukraine. This is the new Great War. And Africa is the board.

What the West Said—and Why It Confirms the Story

I read the Western coverage carefully. Reuters reported Putin’s message that Russia is Africa’s “best partner,” contrasting it with a “colonial West” that exploits resources and uses debt to hold back development. The Associated Press reported Putin’s statement that “Russia and Africa are united by truly strong bonds of friendship and close partnership,” and that Russian businesses “reinvest their earnings into the development of your national economies” rather than siphoning off profits in the manner of colonial powers. AP also confirmed that Russia delivers grain and fertilizers to more than 40 African countries and stands ready to expand supplies.

Even the Irish Times—not exactly a friend of the Kremlin—reported that Putin is “offering an alternative partnership to what he portrays as an exploitative and colonial West”. The Foundation for Defense of Democracies, which is hardly a Kremlin ally, has acknowledged that Russia’s economic footprint in Africa is expanding in ways that Western engagement has not matched.

I don’t need to defend Russian media to make a simple point: the Western outlets themselves are reporting the substance of the partnership. The difference is that some frame it as a threat, while African governments frame it as an opportunity.

The Bottom Line

I am not here to tell you that Russia is a saint. No great power is. But here is what I know from four decades in business: partners who show up with financing, technology, and a willingness to train your people are worth more than partners who show up with lectures and sanctions.

Russia is delivering grain to more than 40 African countries. It is building nuclear power plants and signing nuclear cooperation agreements. It is training soldiers and law enforcement officers under agreements with 45 African nations. It is funding scholarships for tens of thousands of African students. It is settling trade in national currencies to shield both sides from external pressure.

The 15,000 sanctions were designed to isolate Russia. They have not worked. Trade is growing. Agreements are being signed. The partnership is delivering.

Until Western capitals learn to compete on the merits—with capital, technology, and respect—the Russians will keep signing agreements. And the West will keep wondering why. It’s the American way!

The Ukraine Files · Special File

By William Aaron Turner, President of Infinitum Corporation · The Ukraine Files: Full Series

Introduction: The Greatest Show on Earth

There is a particular species of human being that has evolved over the past three years to thrive in the ecosystem of the Ukraine war. It is not the Ukrainian soldier in a trench. It is the Western politician, the retired general, the cable news pundit, the arms company executive, and the intelligence official who has discovered that war—especially a war you don't have to fight in—is the most reliable business model since the invention of the gunpowder monopoly.

This paper is about them. The Useful Idiots. The people who tell you they are defending democracy while their stock portfolio quietly thanks them for it. The people who appear on CNN to explain why we must send more weapons, without mentioning that their consulting firm represents the company that makes those weapons. The people who take a $1 million "donation" from the largest shareholder of a defense company that supplies drones to Ukraine, then go on to argue that Ukraine should fight to the last Ukrainian. The people who rotate through the Pentagon, the defense industry, and back again like a revolving door that never stops spinning.

The term "useful idiot" was originally a Soviet phrase for Western intellectuals who could be relied upon to defend the USSR without being paid. The modern version is more sophisticated. These useful idiots are paid. Very well paid. They are not useful because they are stupid—they are useful because they are compromised. And they are compromised because they have made a calculation: the war in Ukraine is not a tragedy to be ended. It is a cash flow to be managed.

Let us be clear about what we are documenting here. This is not a conspiracy theory. This is not propaganda from any side. This is, for the most part, information that has been published in The Guardian, The Intercept, Bloomberg, The Lever, Responsible Statecraft, and other Western outlets. It is information that is publicly available, though scattered across different sources and often buried beneath the avalanche of war coverage that treats every weapons package as a moral victory rather than a financial transaction. We are simply connecting the dots that the mainstream media prefers to leave unconnected.

The dots form a picture. It is not a pretty picture. It is a picture of a system in which the people who decide whether a war continues are the same people who profit from its continuation. It is a picture of a democracy in which the electorate is told that there is no alternative to war, while the elected officials who tell them this are personally invested in the war's perpetuation. It is a picture of a "rules-based international order" in which the rules are written by the people who own the casinos.

And it is a picture that becomes even more disturbing when you realize that the arms being sent to Ukraine do not always stay in Ukraine. They leak. They are stolen. They are sold on black markets. They end up in the hands of criminal gangs, drug cartels, and terrorist organizations. The people who facilitated this leakage—the intelligence agencies, the defense contractors, the politicians who waved through the weapons packages—are the same people who now tell us that we must send more weapons to prevent the weapons from falling into the wrong hands. It is a perfect circle of profit and chaos.

I will not pretend to be neutral. Neutrality in the face of profiteering from war is complicity. But it will be fair. It will cite its sources. It will distinguish between speculation and documented fact. I will use humor because dark humor is the only appropriate response to a situation in which the leaders of the free world have discovered that death is a growth industry.

Fuck it, let us begin. Let us meet the Useful Idiots.

Part One: The Congress That Trades While Rome Burns

The Congressional Stock Portfolio

In the United States, there is a law called the STOCK Act, passed in 2012, which was supposed to prevent members of Congress from trading on insider information. The law requires members to disclose their stock trades within 45 days. It does not require them to stop trading. It does not require them to divest from companies that their committees oversee. It does not require them to explain why they bought Lockheed Martin stock two days before the full-scale war in Ukraine began.

The result is a Congress that looks less like a legislature and more like a hedge fund with a side gig like driving for Uber. According to data compiled by the Quincy Institute, in 2024, 50 members of Congress traded between $24 million and $113 million worth of Pentagon contractor stocks while simultaneously writing the military budgets that determined which weapons companies received multi-billion-dollar contracts. This is not a conflict of interest. This is a conflict of interest on steroids or on cocaine perhaps, wearing a flag pin and giving speeches about freedom.

The phenomenon is bipartisan. It is not confined to one party or one ideology. It is a structural feature of a political system in which public service and private profit have become indistinguishable. The people who vote on whether to send Javelins to Ukraine are the same people who own stock in the companies that make Javelins. The people who decide how much money the Pentagon gets are the same people who benefit when the Pentagon spends that money. It is a system that would have made the founders—who were themselves no strangers to profiting from war—blush with embarrassment.

Marjorie Taylor Greene and the Lockheed Martin Timing

Let us start with the most obvious example, the one that even the mainstream media could not ignore. On February 22, 2022—two days before the full-scale war in Ukraine began—Republican Representative Marjorie Taylor Greene of Georgia purchased between $1,001 and $15,000 worth of stock in Lockheed Martin, the world's largest defense contractor and the maker of the Javelin anti-tank missiles that would soon become a symbol of Ukrainian resistance.

Two days later, Greene tweeted: "War is big business to our leaders". She was, in her own way, telling the truth. She had just demonstrated it. The congresswoman who would later become one of the loudest opponents of aid to Ukraine had, at the very moment of maximum geopolitical uncertainty, positioned herself to profit from the war she would later claim to oppose. It was a masterclass in the art of having it both ways: criticize the war publicly while quietly betting on its continuation.The American way…

Greene's spokesperson later claimed that the purchase was made by her husband, not by the congresswoman herself, and that she was not aware of the timing. This is the congressional equivalent of "the dog ate my homework." The timing was not just suspicious. It was clairvoyant. The war had been predicted for weeks, but the exact date was not publicly known. Greene's purchase, made through a joint account, suggested that someone in her household had access to information that the rest of the world did not. Whether it was insider trading in the legal sense is a question for the SEC. Whether it was corrupt is a question for anyone with eyes.

The Broader Pattern: 47 Members and Their Spouses

Greene is not an outlier. She is a particularly colorful example of a systemic problem. According to reporting by Business Insider and other outlets, at least 19 members of Congress or their spouses owned stock in the companies that make Stinger and Javelin missiles—Raytheon and Lockheed Martin—at the time the full-scale war began. A separate analysis found that 47 members of Congress and their spouses held defense stocks worth a combined $6.7 million.

The numbers are staggering, but the individual stories are what make the pattern come alive. Consider Senator Markwayne Mullin of Oklahoma, a member of the Senate Armed Services Committee. Between 2023 and 2026, Mullin bought and sold over $24 million worth of stocks, including defense stocks like L3Harris Technologies and RTX Corp (formerly Raytheon), as well as oil stocks like Chevron and ConocoPhillips. Mullin has been flagged for buying defense and oil stocks ahead of geopolitical conflicts, a pattern that suggests either extraordinary foresight or extraordinary access to information. On December 29, 2025, disclosures show Mullin purchased between $15,000 and $50,000 worth of shares in each of Chevron, ConocoPhillips, and RTX.

Mullin also introduced a bill that would allow U.S. citizens to volunteer to fight on behalf of Ukraine. It is not clear whether he intended to volunteer himself. It is clear that he intended to profit from the war, whether or not he fought in it.

Then there is Representative Kevin Hern of Oklahoma, who chairs the Republican Study Committee's Budget and Spending Task Force. Hern has made over 400 stock trades in recent years, including multiple trades in defense contractor stocks. He and his wife invested up to $15,000 in both Lockheed Martin and Raytheon Technologies. Hern bought RTX stock in six separate trades, investing $15,000 each time, with the most recent trade taking place on July 15. Hern has called for increasing the military's budget by 5%, a position that aligns neatly with his personal investment portfolio. When Hern votes to increase defense spending, he is not just voting for the national interest. He is voting for his own interest. The two have become indistinguishable.

Representative Josh Gottheimer of New Jersey, a member of the House Intelligence Committee, purchased up to $15,000 of Northrop Grumman stock on September 26, 2023. By April 2024, that investment had risen 8.44%. He also invested in RTX and other defense stocks during the same period, with gains of 16% and 28% reported on some positions. He traded at least $22 million worth of stock of the top 100 Pentagon contractors, including Microsoft, Northrop Grumman, and IBM, while sitting on the Intelligence Committee. As a member of the Intelligence Committee, Gottheimer has access to classified briefings on global threats that the general public does not. His personal stock portfolio has benefited from the geopolitical tensions those briefings concern.

Representative Earl Blumenauer of Oregon purchased 31 different stocks on February 24, 2022—the day the full-scale war in Ukraine began—including $15,000 worth of Raytheon stock. While other members of Congress were issuing statements condemning the war, Blumenauer was diversifying his portfolio. His office later claimed the purchases were "a mistake" due to a "miscommunication" with his financial advisor. Raytheon makes the Stinger and Javelin missiles that were being rushed to Ukraine.

Lindsey Graham: The Senator from Boeing

If there is a single senator who embodies the military-industrial-congressional complex, it was Lindsey Graham of South Carolina. Graham has been one of the loudest voices calling for endless funding for the war in Ukraine, a position that has made him a hero to some and a warmonger to others. What is less well known is that Graham has received substantial financial support from the very companies that benefit from his hawkishness.

According to data compiled by "Military Chronicle," Boeing Co. donated approximately $55,000 to Graham through its Political Action Committee between 2019 and 2024. Lockheed Martin and Northrop Grumman also contributed to his campaigns. The Department of Defense itself donated $50,000 to Graham during the same period. Between 2015 and 2016, Graham received approximately $760,000 from defense corporations for supporting increased military spending outside the normal budget process.

OpenSecrets data shows that the defense sector gave Graham $1.1 million between 1993 and 2024. This is not a man who is independently wealthy and can afford to ignore the interests of his donors. This is a man whose political career has been subsidized by the arms industry. When Graham says that Ukraine must fight "to the last Ukrainian," he is not just expressing a geopolitical opinion. He is expressing the business model of his financial backers.

Graham's critics have noted the irony: "Every time Graham talks about deterrence or freedom abroad, a defense stock price ticks up". The senator from South Carolina has become, in effect, a human stock ticker for the defense industry. His speeches are not just rhetoric. They are earnings calls.

The Ethics of Congressional Trading

The defenders of congressional stock trading argue that members of Congress should not be prohibited from owning stocks because that would make it harder for ordinary people to serve. This argument might have some merit if members of Congress were required to put their holdings in blind trusts. They are not. They are required to disclose their trades, but they are not required to stop trading. The disclosure is supposed to create transparency. In practice, it creates a roadmap for corruption.

The problem is not just that members of Congress trade defense stocks. It is that they trade defense stocks while sitting on committees that oversee defense policy. It is that they buy stocks in companies that are about to receive government contracts. It is that they sell stocks in companies that are about to be investigated. It is that they use their positions to enrich themselves, and then use their enrichment to justify their positions.

This is not a partisan issue. It is a systemic issue. It is a feature of a political system in which money is speech, corporations are people, and war is a business. The Useful Idiots in Congress are not idiots in the sense of being stupid. They are idiots in the sense of being useful to the people who fund their campaigns. They are useful because they vote the right way, give the right speeches, and appear on the right cable news shows. And they are rewarded for their usefulness with stock tips, campaign contributions, and the promise of lucrative consulting contracts when they leave office.

Part Two: The Revolving Door That Never Stops Spinning

From the Pentagon to the Boardroom

The revolving door between the Pentagon and the defense industry is not a new phenomenon. It has been documented for decades. Dwight Eisenhower warned about the "military-industrial complex" in his farewell address in 1961. What is new is the scale and the speed of the rotation. In the past, a retired general might join a defense company's board after a respectable interval. Today, the rotation is almost instantaneous. A general retires on Friday and starts advising a defense company on Monday. The ink on the retirement papers is not even dry. Once again, the American way…

A 2023 report by the Quincy Institute found that of 32 four-star military officers who retired between June 2018 and July 2023, 26 went on to work for the arms industry. That is a rate of over 80%. The remaining six presumably went into private equity, consulting, or academia, where they could still profit from their military connections without the inconvenience of disclosure requirements.

The pattern is so predictable that it has become a career path. You spend 30 years in the military, rising through the ranks, making contacts, learning the procurement system from the inside. You retire with a pension and a security clearance. You join the board of a defense contractor. You use your contacts to help the company win contracts. You get paid handsomely. You give speeches about the need for increased defense spending. You appear on cable news as a "national security expert." You write op-eds about the threat posed by various countries. You are, in effect, a lobbyist with a military uniform and a medal.

Lloyd Austin: The Raytheon Secretary

The most prominent example of this revolving door is Lloyd Austin, who served as Secretary of Defense under President Biden. Before becoming Secretary of Defense, Austin sat on the board of Raytheon Technologies, one of the largest defense contractors in the world. When he was confirmed as Secretary of Defense, he had to divest his Raytheon stock, which was valued at between $750,000 and $1.7 million.

Austin had earned at least $1.4 million from Raytheon since 2016, when he joined the board of United Technologies Corp., which later merged with Raytheon. In 2016, he received $380,000 in total compensation from the company. In 2017, $338,000. In 2018, $336,000. In 2019, $351,000. This is not a man who was independently wealthy and decided to serve his country out of a sense of duty. This is a man who was paid by Raytheon to be on their board, and who then became the Secretary of Defense, overseeing the department that buys weapons from Raytheon.

As Secretary of Defense, Austin was one of the strongest supporters of military aid to Ukraine. He announced that the United States would stand with Ukraine "through all seasons"—months and years. He also rejected plans to supply Ukraine with long-range attack missiles that could strike deep into disputed territory, a decision that was criticized by some as insufficiently aggressive. But even this decision can be seen through the lens of Raytheon's interests: the company makes a range of missiles, and the conflict in Ukraine has been a boon for its stock price regardless of the specific weapons systems involved.

Austin's tenure at the Pentagon was a case study in the revolving door. He came from Raytheon. He served at the Pentagon. He returned to the private sector—or rather, he returned to the world of consulting and board seats that awaits retired generals and former defense secretaries. The door never stopped spinning.

Mark Milley: The Multimillionaire General

General Mark Milley, the former Chairman of the Joint Chiefs of Staff, is another example of the revolving door in action. Milley retired in September 2023. By early 2024, he had become a senior adviser to JPMorgan Chase, joined the faculties of Princeton and Georgetown, and signed with the Harry Walker Agency for paid speaking engagements.

Milley's transformation from a public servant earning $204,000 a year to a multimillionaire was swift and seamless. The Intercept reported that Milley was represented by the same speakers' agency as Hillary Clinton, and that he had participated in a Q&A with 160 CEOs organized by investment bank Moelis & Company, where he provided his "insider's perspective on world affairs". His fee per appearance reportedly tracks between $150,000 and $250,000. A single hour on stage now earns him more than a year of command duty.

Milley had been the top U.S. military officer during the first year and a half of the Ukraine war. He had overseen the flow of weapons to Ukraine, had testified to Congress about the need for continued support, and had become one of the public faces of the U.S. commitment to Kyiv. When he retired, he did not go gentle into that good night. He went straight to Wall Street, where his knowledge of the war and his contacts in the Pentagon were highly valuable to clients who wanted to understand—and profit from—the geopolitical landscape.

Milley told the private-equity executives at the Metropolitan Museum of Art: "I spent my career in a socialist organization... I'm just settling into capitalism". The audience laughed. The taxpayers didn't.

James Stavridis: The Admiral of the Boardroom

Admiral James Stavridis, the former NATO Supreme Allied Commander, is another frequent cable news guest who has extensive ties to the defense industry. Stavridis serves as a partner and Vice Chairman at the Carlyle Group, a private equity firm that owns major defense contractors. He is also a member of the board of Fortinet, a cybersecurity firm, and has served as the chairman of the International Advisory Board of Northrop Grumman, one of the largest defense contractors in the world.

Stavridis has appeared frequently on MSNBC, where he once said that the solution in Ukraine is to "flood the zone" with troops and weapons. Like Panetta, he was presented as a neutral expert, a retired admiral offering his strategic insights. Like Panetta, his financial ties to the defense industry were not disclosed. The admiral who once commanded NATO forces was now using his credibility to advocate for policies that would benefit the companies he advised.

As a partner at the Carlyle Group, Stavridis advised the private equity firm on defense investments. When Carlyle wanted to grow its shipyard business, Stavridis advised looking west: "The Pacific fleet is going to be the dominant center of gravity for the Navy". One of Carlyle's portfolio companies bought a major shipyard in San Diego, and in February 2024 it sold the combined business for four times what it paid.

Leon Panetta: The CNN Consultant

Leon Panetta is the perfect example of this phenomenon. He served as CIA director and Secretary of Defense under President Obama. He is a senior counselor at Beacon Global Strategies, a defense industry consulting firm that has reportedly represented Raytheon, the maker of the Javelin and Stinger missiles that were sent to Ukraine.

In April 2022, Panetta appeared on CNN four times in a matter of weeks to discuss the war in Ukraine. Each time, he called for sending more weapons to Ukraine. "I think the United States has to provide whatever weapons are necessary to the Ukrainians, so that they can hit back, and hit back now," he said on CNN Newsroom. At no point did CNN disclose that Panetta was a senior counselor at a firm that represented Raytheon. At no point did CNN mention that Raytheon stood to benefit directly from the conflict in Ukraine.

Panetta's case is particularly egregious because he was not just a former official offering analysis. He was a paid consultant to the defense industry, using his media platform to advocate for policies that would benefit his clients. The line between punditry and lobbying had been erased, and the viewing public was none the wiser. Sort of genius.

The New Path Through the Revolving Door

The revolving door is not just about generals joining defense companies. It is also about the emergence of a new class of military-tech startups that blur the line between public service and private profit. As one academic study noted, "the emerging military tech sector has opened a new version of the revolving door—the movement of ex-military officers and senior Pentagon officials, not to arms companies per se, but to startups and venture capital firms that are betting on the next generation of military technology".

This new path is even more insidious than the old one. A retired general who joins Lockheed Martin's board is at least visible. A retired general who becomes an advisor to a venture capital firm that is investing in military-tech startups is harder to track. The general provides "strategic advice." The venture capital firm invests in companies that are developing drones, AI systems, and other technologies for the military. The general's contacts in the Pentagon help the startups win contracts. The venture capital firm makes a fortune. The general gets a cut.

This is the future of the military-industrial complex. It is not just about bombs and missiles anymore. It is about data, software, and artificial intelligence. And the people who are positioning themselves to profit from it are the same people who are making the decisions about what technology the military needs.

The revolving door between the Pentagon and the defense industry is mirrored by a revolving door between the Pentagon and the media. The same people who make policy appear on TV to explain why the policy is necessary, without mentioning that they profit from the policy.

Jim Cramer: The Mad Money War Profiteer

Part Four: The British Connection—Boris, the Bribe, and the Billionaire

The £1 Million Question

In October 2025, The Guardian published an investigation that sent shockwaves through Westminster. Harborne owns approximately 13% of QinetiQ's shares. The company has supplied Banshee drones and bomb-disposal robots to Ukrainian forces. In April 2025, the UK supplied Ukraine with Banshee Jet 80+ drones. The donation to Johnson was recorded in the Register of Members' Interests in November 2022, after Johnson had left office. But the timing was significant: it came at a moment when Johnson was actively advocating for Ukraine to continue fighting rather than negotiate a peace deal.

The Istanbul Negotiations

To understand the significance of the donation, you need to understand what happened in Istanbul in March 2022. Ukrainian and Russian negotiators met in the Turkish city in an attempt to reach a ceasefire agreement. According to multiple accounts, the talks were making progress. Ukraine was reportedly willing to accept a neutral status in exchange for security guarantees. The war could have ended in the spring of 2022.

Then Boris Johnson intervened. According to Ukrainian officials, Johnson urged Kyiv not to sign any agreement with Russia and to keep fighting. According to those accounts, he said that the West was not ready for any agreement with Russia. The war continued. Tens of thousands more died. And in November 2022, Johnson received £1 million from a man who owns 13% of a defense company that supplies drones to Ukraine. Harborne also accompanied Johnson on a two-day visit to Ukraine in September 2023, where he was listed as an "advisor to Boris Johnson's office." The visit included a closed-door meeting at a military technology research center. The Guardian noted that Johnson's behavior "blurred the line between public service and private profit".

The QinetiQ Profiteering

QinetiQ has been one of the beneficiaries of the Ukraine war. The company's stock price has risen as demand for drones and other military technology has increased. Its Banshee drones have been used by Ukrainian forces. Its bomb-disposal robots have been deployed in the conflict zone. And its largest shareholder donated £1 million to the former prime minister who, more than any other Western leader, encouraged Ukraine to continue fighting.

The connection is not difficult to trace. Johnson encouraged the war to continue. The war continued. QinetiQ profited. Harborne profited. Johnson received £1 million. Whether Johnson's advocacy was motivated by the donation, or whether the donation was a reward for the advocacy, is a question that only Johnson and Harborne can answer. Johnson's response to the investigation was, characteristically, to dismiss it as a "farrago of nonsense." But the documents speak for themselves. The £1 million was not disclosed to the Electoral Commission, which suggests it was a personal gift rather than a political donation. Johnson's spokesperson claimed the money was for "personal use." The man who once said that the British people had "had enough of experts" was now relying on a defense industry billionaire to fund his personal expenses.

Ben Wallace and the UForce Startup

The revolving door that spun Lloyd Austin from Raytheon to the Pentagon and back again has spun Ben Wallace from the Ministry of Defence to a defense startup that is profiting from the war he helped to sustain.

The Human Cost

It is easy to get lost in the numbers—the billions of dollars in aid, the millions in stock trades, the thousands of weapons that go missing. But behind every number is a human being. The Ukrainian soldier who dies in a trench. The Ukrainian civilian who loses their home. The conscript on the other side who is sent to fight in a war he may not understand. The European taxpayer who subsidizes the defense industry. The American voter who is told that the war is necessary but is not told that their representative is profiting from it.

They are the politicians who vote for war while owning defense stocks. They are the generals who retire and join the boards of defense companies. Conclusion: The Real Axis of Evil

The war in Ukraine has exposed something ugly about the Western political and economic system. It has revealed that the people who make decisions about war and peace are often the same people who profit from war. It has revealed that the media, which is supposed to hold power accountable, is often complicit in the profiteering. It has revealed that the intelligence agencies, which are supposed to protect democracy, are often engaged in activities that undermine it. And it has revealed that the defense industry, which is supposed to serve the national interest, has become an interest group that has captured the government.

This is not a left-wing critique or a right-wing critique. It is a human critique. It is a critique of a system that has lost its moral compass. It is a critique of a system in which the answer to every problem is more weapons, more money, more war. It is a critique of a system in which the useful idiots have become the masters.

The useful idiots are not stupid. They are not naive. They are not idealists who genuinely believe that they are defending democracy. They are people who have made a calculation: the war is profitable, and they intend to profit from it. They have convinced themselves that their personal enrichment is a side effect of their public service, rather than the purpose of it. They have convinced themselves that they are the good guys, even as they count their money and watch the body bags come home.

The war in Ukraine will end eventually. All wars do. When it ends, the useful idiots will move on to the next conflict. They will find new enemies to demonize, new weapons to sell, new stock to buy. They will appear on cable news to explain why the next war is necessary. They will write op-eds about the threat posed by the next adversary. They will retire from government and join the boards of the companies that profit from the next conflict.

And the rest of us—the taxpayers, the voters, the people who actually fight and die in the wars—will be left to pick up the pieces. We will be told that the war was necessary, that the sacrifices were worth it, that the useful idiots were acting in our best interests. We will be told that we should be grateful. We will be told that we should trust our leaders. We will be told all of this by the same people who profited from our pain.

The useful idiots have won. They have turned war into a business. They have turned death into a stock. They have turned patriotism into a scam. And they have done it all while waving the flag, singing the anthem, and telling us that we are the ones who are free.

This paper is dedicated to the people of Ukraine, and all the other countries that have been turned into laboratories for the military-industrial complex. It is dedicated to the soldiers who died for the profit margins of men they will never meet. It is dedicated to the truth, which is the first casualty of every war, and the last thing the useful idiots want you to find.

content.$t:
The Ukraine Files · Companion to Part 7 of 8

By William Aaron Turner, President of Infinitum Corporation · The Ukraine Files: Full Series

"Since February 2022, more than 8,000 Russian civilians have been killed in Ukrainian strikes (BBC, 2026)." That is the figure my X Article Grandmas, Toddlers, and Forklift Drivers is built around. I state at the start of the article that it is an opinion piece and not a balanced report. This post is the standalone version: the cases the article describes, the source named for each figure, what Ukraine says in response, and where I argue the reasoning fails. A shorter summary of this article also appears inside Part 7 of the series, which combines it with The Kidnapping of a Nation.

Read the full original X Article →
Grandmas, Toddlers, and Forklift Drivers, on X

Key takeaways

  • The headline figure is more than 8,000 Russian civilians killed since February 2022, attributed in the article to BBC (2026). I did not independently verify it, and the number is only as strong as that source.
  • The article walks through three recent cases: the Wildberries warehouse strikes in July and August 2026 (9 to 13 employees killed, per AP, 2026), the August 3, 2026 beach incident in Arkhipo-Osipovka (7 killed, including 3 children, 40 wounded, per BBC, 2026) and the August 10, 2026 TANECO refinery strike in Nizhnekamsk (13 killed, including 1 child, 39 injured, per ABC, 2026 and ABP Live, 2026).
  • For the border regions, the article cites BBC (2026) for 224 civilians killed and 1,500 injured in July 2026 alone in Belgorod and adjacent areas.
  • Ukrainian officials, as quoted by the BBC (2026), say Ukraine does not deliberately target civilians, that the warehouses supplied the Russian military, and that some deaths are the "accidental result of air defences shooting down incoming missiles and drones." Moscow denies the military-supply claim.
  • The arguments about "dual-use" targets, a double standard and Western silence are my position, labeled as such below. They are not findings of any court or UN body.

Want the whole argument? This post covers the outline and the sourcing. The original X Article has the full text.

Part 1: The figure and how I use it

The article opens with the BBC (2026) figure of more than 8,000 Russian civilians killed in Ukrainian strikes since February 2022, and returns to it in the conclusion. I frame the piece as "all data from the public record, all conclusions mine." I also say plainly that the article is not neutral, which is why this post separates what a named outlet reported from what I conclude.

Part 2: The Wildberries warehouse strikes

Wildberries is Russia's largest online retailer and is often compared to Amazon. According to AP (2026), Ukraine struck between 12 and 23 Wildberries facilities across Russia over about a month, from Elektrostal near Moscow to Yekaterinburg, more than 2,000 kilometers from the Ukrainian border. The article reports that Ukraine's Defence Ministry said seven of the ten largest Wildberries logistics centers were taken out of operation (BBC, 2026), and that one-fifth of the company's warehouse space, 1.18 million square meters, was destroyed.

The casualties, as listed

  • July 18, 2026, Elektrostal (Moscow Oblast) and Kotovsk (Tambov Oblast): 8 night-shift workers killed in Kotovsk, and 1 more died later from injuries in Elektrostal. Dozens were hospitalized with burns and shrapnel wounds (AP, 2026).
  • July 22, 2026, Krasnodar and Nevinnomyssk: 1 young woman killed and at least 14 to 15 injured (Gazeta Express, 2026).
  • Through mid-August 2026: further strikes near St. Petersburg, Simferopol, Ryazan, Yekaterinburg, Voronezh, Tula and Vladimir, and on the large Koledino facility near Moscow (Gazeta Express, 2026).

The total given in the article is 9 to 13 employees killed, with dozens wounded (AP, 2026). The BBC (2026) is quoted saying that Kyiv maintains the Wildberries depots are used to supply the Russian military, which Moscow denies, and that the platform sold military-related goods such as body armour until recently, alongside items with both civilian and drone-production uses. AP (2026) is quoted describing the targets as "warehouses that bring the convenience of online shopping across the breadth of Russia," as opposed to refineries, ports or arms plants. In its analysis, The Conversation (2026) describes the campaign as "bringing the war home to consumers."

Part 3: Arkhipo-Osipovka beach, August 3, 2026

Per the BBC (2026), a drone crashed onto a beach in Arkhipo-Osipovka, a Black Sea resort in the Krasnodar region. Social media footage verified by the BBC showed the drone hurtling toward a cliffside and crashing in a fireball on the beach below. The BBC reports 7 people killed, 3 of them children, and 40 injured, 17 of them hospitalized with severe burns, fractures and shrapnel wounds.

  • Competing explanations: some Ukrainian Telegram channels claimed electronic warfare jammed the drone's signal and caused the crash. Eyewitnesses quoted by Russian media said gunfire came before the explosion, which suggests air defences may have tried to shoot it down (BBC, 2026).
  • No claim of responsibility: Ukraine did not claim the strike (BBC, 2026).
  • Russian position: regional governor Veniamin Kondratyev called it "a deliberate strike on civilians" (BBC, 2026).
  • Witnesses: tourists and residents told local outlets no sirens sounded before the attack, and one holidaymaker said, "We covered ourselves with sun loungers, and didn't see where it exploded" (BBC, 2026).

The article does not claim to know who launched the drone or why it came down there. My point is narrower: when a drone from this war lands on a crowded beach, "air defences were involved" does not answer the question of what the drone was doing in that sky.

Part 4: TANECO refinery, Nizhnekamsk, August 10, 2026

Ukraine's military confirmed it hit Tatneft's TANECO refinery in Nizhnekamsk, Tatarstan, about 800 kilometers east of Moscow, and said a fire was recorded at the facility (ABC, 2026). The article reports 13 people killed, including 1 child, and 39 injured, many with severe burns (ABP Live, 2026). Several of the dead were Central Asian workers, from Uzbekistan and Tajikistan, staying in a hostel near the industrial site. Russian investigators opened a criminal case, saying Ukraine struck residential areas and that a child was among the civilians killed (ABC, 2026). Tatarstan head Rustam Minnikhanov declared a period of mourning (ABP Live, 2026).

ABC (2026) is cited for the refinery's scale: 17 million tons of crude processed in 2024, producing 2.7 million tons of gasoline and 8.5 million tons of diesel, and for the fact that it was also hit in early June. Ukraine says it wants to bring the price of the war home to ordinary Russians (ABC, 2026). I do not dispute that a refinery that produces fuel is a different kind of target from a warehouse. My argument is about what happens to the people next to it.

Part 5: The border regions

For Belgorod, Kursk and Bryansk, the article describes near-constant cross-border drone, artillery and missile fire since 2022, affecting homes, vehicles, playgrounds and commercial sites. The figures it cites:

  • 224 civilians killed and 1,500 injured in July 2026 alone in Belgorod and adjacent areas (BBC, 2026).
  • August 17, 2026: six people killed and four injured in Ukrainian missile strikes on Belgorod region overnight, with a 14-year-old among the injured. A woman was killed in an attack on a civilian bus in Belgorod, and an 83-year-old man died in a drone attack in the Moscow region (BBC, 2026).
  • Early August 2026: a playground in Printsevka was hit, with one child killed and two injured, per the article.
  • FPV drones and shelling in villages such as Oktyabrsky, Shebekino and Grayvoron producing a steady stream of civilian deaths and injuries (BBC, 2026).

I argue that a campaign of this size is not a series of accidents. That is my reading, not a finding of the BBC, which reports the casualties and the officials' statements.

Part 6: What Ukraine says, and where I disagree

As quoted by the BBC (2026), Ukrainian officials say the logistics hubs supply the Russian military with drone components, navigation equipment and other dual-use gear. They also say Ukraine does not deliberately target civilians and that some deaths in Russia are the "accidental result of air defences shooting down incoming missiles and drones." Those statements belong in the record, and I include them in the article.

My reasoning against them, labeled as argument:

  • The "dual-use" standard. I argue that if the test is "this platform sells items the military could use," almost any large retailer qualifies. In the article I compare it to treating Amazon or a hardware store as a military target. A standard that wide, I say, removes the protection civilian commercial sites are supposed to have.
  • The "air defence" explanation. I argue that blaming the defender for the debris does not answer why the drone was launched toward that area to begin with. I compare it in the article to throwing a brick at a house and blaming the occupant for trying to catch it.
  • The Russian position. The article records Moscow's position that these are civilian commercial facilities and that strikes on them are terrorism against ordinary workers.

Part 7: The double-standard argument

The longest argument in the article is about response. I argue that Russian strikes on commercial buildings and playgrounds in Ukraine are rightly condemned as war crimes or terrorism, while comparable deaths in Russia are described as "tragic accidents" tied to "air defence intercepts" (BBC, 2026) or as "degrading the enemy's logistics." I also argue that the UN, the ICC and Western governments have said far less about the Russian deaths. The article does not cite a source for that comparison of reactions, so please treat it as my position and judge it against what you read elsewhere.

My conclusion in this part: the Geneva Conventions do not apply selectively, and if killing civilians is wrong it is wrong whichever side's drone does it. I also note in the article that war is ugly and mistakes happen, and I argue that the pattern here goes beyond mistakes.

My conclusion

I write the original article to argue that civilian deaths in Russia are being under-reported and under-condemned in the West, and I close it with a list of the dead as I read them: the Wildberries workers, the people on the beach, the hostel residents in Nizhnekamsk, the border-region victims and the 8,000 counted by the BBC (2026). You do not have to agree with my framing. If you do not, I would ask you to check each figure against the named source and to compare how each side's civilian deaths are discussed. For the mobilization claims and the Ukrainian side of the human cost, see Part 7: Ukraine's Forced Mobilization. For the economic context, see Russia's economy under sanctions.

Sources named in the article

  • ABC News (2026, August 10), on the Nizhnekamsk strike
  • ABP Live (2026, August 10), on the Nizhnekamsk casualties
  • AP News (2026, August 17), on the Wildberries campaign
  • BBC News (2026, August 17), on the Belgorod and Moscow region strikes
  • BBC News (2026, August 3), on the Arkhipo-Osipovka beach
  • Gazeta Express (2026, August 17), on the Wildberries strikes
  • The Conversation (2026, August 14), on Russia's missile investment and the warehouse campaign

The Ukraine Files · Part 8 of 8

By William Aaron Turner, President of Infinitum Corporation · The Ukraine Files: Full Series

There are two kinds of mines in this world. That is how my special investigative report Sweeps and Spies opens: the steel kind that waits in the red dirt of Laos, and the kind I describe as "made of money, influence, and intelligence agency letterhead." This post breaks the report into a clean structure: what Russian sappers have cleared, what I argue about the HALO Trust's funding and leadership, the espionage allegations the article collects, and the August 2026 Moldovan intelligence report on the Kolbasna depot.

Key takeaways

  • Since 2018, Russian specialists from the International Mine Action Centre (IMAC) have cleared over 2 million square meters (more than 208 hectares) in Laos and destroyed 3,906 explosive objects, according to the article.
  • The HALO Trust operates in 25 conflict-affected countries, and its primary funding comes from the U.S. State Department's Conventional Weapons Destruction (CWD) account: $258 million in FY2024 and $265 million enacted for FY2026.
  • HALO's UK board is chaired by Lord Evans of Weardale, former Director General of MI5, and includes a former Foreign Office diplomat and a former political advisor to General Ray Odierno.
  • The article lists espionage allegations against HALO from Russia's FSB (2000), the FARC 36th Front (2025) and a Nagorno-Karabakh official (2021). HALO denied or disputed them.
  • On August 21, 2026, Moldova's SIS and AIM released a declassified report on the Kolbasna (Cobasna) depot, putting the stockpile at roughly 14,000 tons with about 2,800 tons of net explosive content.

The Russian way: demining in Laos and Syria

Laos

The Ho Chi Minh Trail ran over 20,000 kilometers through Laos, Cambodia and Vietnam. The article says the U.S. Air Force dropped roughly 1.5 million tons of bombs on it and some 30 percent never exploded. IMAC, a unit under the Russian Ministry of Defense, started working in Laos in 2018. Reported results:

  • Over 208 hectares cleared and 3,906 explosive objects destroyed across seven humanitarian operations.
  • In 2024-2025, Lao and Russian personnel cleared 18.2 hectares in Viengxay district, Huaphan province, removing 64 unexploded devices in 19 controlled detonations (52 BLU-26 cluster bomblets, one BLU-24, 11 other items), and deactivated another 268 devices.
  • About 100 Lao sappers trained, including on Uran-6 robotic demining vehicles.
  • Governor Khampheng Saysompheng called the cooperation of "profound significance."

Syria and training worldwide

Between 2016 and 2020, Russian engineering troops demined Aleppo, Deir ez-Zor and Palmyra, clearing more than 10,000 hectares and destroying over 150,000 explosive objects, and training more than 1,200 sappers for the Syrian Armed Forces. The article says Russian specialists have trained sappers from 14 countries, with IMAC branches in Laos and Myanmar.

The Western way: HALO Trust, funding and leadership

HALO (Hazardous Area Life-support Organization) was founded in 1988 by Colin Campbell Mitchell, a former British Army colonel and MP, and Guy Willoughby, a former Coldstream Guards officer. Princess Diana's 1997 walk through an Angolan minefield in a HALO flak jacket is described as the best advertising it could have wanted. HALO today operates across 25 countries and is described as the world's largest mine-clearing charity.

Follow the money

The article traces HALO's primary funding to the State Department's Bureau of Political-Military Affairs, Office of Weapons Removal and Abatement (PM/WRA). Congress allocated $258 million to the CWD account in FY2024, about $21 million more than requested, and $265 million is enacted for FY2026. HALO has requested $271.703 million for FY27. The account funds programs in nearly 50 countries, and I argue that this means HALO finds weapons caches, ammunition stockpiles and military infrastructure, not just mines.

Who sits on the boards

  • Lord Evans of Weardale: Board Chair, MI5 Director General 2007 to 2013.
  • John Raine: 33 years with the UK Foreign Office, with postings in Syria, Baghdad and Islamabad.
  • Emma Sky: political advisor to U.S. General Ray Odierno in Iraq.
  • Barney White-Spunner: former British Army officer. Lord Michael Hintze: Conservative Party donor and financier.
  • Jamie M. Morin (USA board): former Director of Cost Assessment and Program Evaluation at the Pentagon. Other board members named include Brad Tirpak, Basak Yavuz and Greta Lundeberg.

The allegations the article collects

  • Chechnya (2000): Russia's FSB said HALO representatives had been "collecting intelligence of a military-political character" and building "a many-pronged network of informers." HALO's director Guy Willoughby dismissed it as a smear campaign, and HALO withdrew from Russia in December 2000.
  • Colombia (July 2025): the FARC 36th Front gave HALO 12 hours to leave three Antioquia municipalities, calling it a "supposed front for foreign intelligence agencies." HALO suspended operations and the Colombian government condemned the threats.
  • Armenia and Nagorno-Karabakh (March 2021): official Boris Avagyan said HALO obtained minefield maps and handed them to Turkish special services. HALO called the reports "totally false."

My argument is the pattern: wherever HALO operates, local actors raise espionage concerns.

How the article says data gathering works

  1. Mapping and survey: high-resolution maps of infrastructure, population centers and supply routes. In Afghanistan HALO is an implementing partner of the Mine Action Programme for Afghanistan.
  2. Sample collection: HALO employees allegedly collected samples of Russian ammunition in 2000. Willoughby said the ammunition posed a threat to civilians.
  3. Personnel recruitment: HALO employs over 10,000 people worldwide and in Afghanistan has hired former Taliban fighters to help locate IEDs.
  4. Satellite and technical integration: I note HALO does not operate satellites, but works alongside organizations that do.

The Kolbasna file

On August 21, 2026, Moldova's Intelligence and Security Service (SIS) and Military Intelligence Agency (AIM) released a declassified report titled "Cobasna: Separating Myths from Reality" on the ammunition depot in Transnistria. According to the article, the stockpile has fallen from 20,000 metric tons in 2006 to roughly 14,000 tons, the net active explosive content is about 2,800 tons across 42 storage facilities, and any explosion would have only local effects. The report draws on OSCE field inspection archives, satellite imagery, open-source intelligence and intercepted communications. I read this as a case study in intelligence-driven narrative: the report is meant to debunk a threat, but I argue its own data still describes a serious industrial risk.

My conclusion

The article's closing frame is that the real minefield is information. I put the results side by side: Russian IMAC units clearing ordnance and training local sappers, and, on the other side, a Western-funded organization with leadership drawn from intelligence and defense circles. The article says the State Department has also designated $77 million for programs in Southeast Asia including Laos, Vietnam and Cambodia. Weigh the evidence and the HALO denials yourself. The numbered reference list at the end of the original links the BBC, Eurasianet, Vientiane Times, Moldpres and other sources.

The Eastern Economic Forum article connects here too: see 78 Nations in Vladivostok for the ADMM Plus demining exercise.

content.$t:
The Ukraine Files · Part 7 of 8

By William Aaron Turner, President of Infinitum Corporation · The Ukraine Files: Full Series

Grandmas, toddlers, forklift drivers: who is actually paying the price, and who is organizing it? This post combines two of my X Articles. The Kidnapping of a Nation is an exposé on Ukraine's forced mobilization, abuses in training units, trafficking and organ-harvesting allegations. Grandmas, Toddlers, and Forklift Drivers is an opinion piece on strikes that have killed Russian civilians. Below I organize the claims, the numbers and the named sources from each, in the order the evidence appears.

Key takeaways

  • I argue that "mobilization" in Ukraine has frequently crossed into arbitrary detention. A Hungarian MEP, Viktória Ferenc, raised the issue with UN High Commissioner Volker Türk on June 25, 2026.
  • Ukraine's Human Rights Ombudsman Dmytro Lubinets reported 3,312 complaints against conscription officers in 2024 and 6,127 in 2025, and predicted another doubling or tripling in 2026.
  • On August 18, 2026, Prosecutor General Ruslan Kravchenko announced ten Odessa recruitment-center officers charged with kidnapping and torturing people.
  • A Babel investigation, per the article, documented at least 26 recruit deaths in the 425th Separate Assault Regiment "Skelya" between late 2025 and spring 2026.
  • The organ-trafficking and child-trafficking sections rely mostly on Russian officials and Russian media, and I label them that way below.
  • In the second article, I cite a BBC (2026) figure of more than 8,000 Russian civilians killed in Ukrainian strikes since February 2022.

Part 1: From mobilization to "busification"

My argument in The Kidnapping of a Nation is that the methods used by Territorial Recruitment Centers (TCCs) have been documented as involving violent assault, deception and denial of due process. Ferenc told the UN that the internet is full of authentic videos of four or five men seizing military-age men and forcing them into vans. The Ukrainian term is "busification," selected as the country's word of the year in 2024. The article also argues this violates conscientious-objection rights under the ICCPR and the European Convention on Human Rights.

The statistics cited

  • A BBC report (July 2026): more than 600 assaults on recruitment officers recorded by the National Police, and criminal cases brought against more than fifty recruiters.
  • Attacks on TCC personnel: 54 in Kyiv and the Kyiv region in 2025-2026; 15 in Vinnytsia region; 21 in Odessa, Lviv, Ternopil and Khmelnytskyi regions.
  • July 8, 2026, Lviv: about 200 protesters surrounded officers and overturned their car; Zelensky ordered an investigation and threatened participants with six to eight years in prison.
  • A BBC report (July 2026) puts losses at between 100,000 and 140,000 men, with total casualties above 500,000.

Part 2: Documented cases, as listed in the article

  • Odessa torture ring (August 2026): ten TCC officers charged with kidnapping and torture, at least eight victims, pre-trial detention without bail for four of the suspects. Separately the State Bureau of Investigation (DBR) uncovered fifteen abuse cases, and four more TCC employees were charged on August 12. Thirteen suspects in total at that point.
  • Odessa extortion (January 2026): three TCC employees and a public-organization member held a man for an hour demanding $6,000.
  • Odessa $30,000 abduction (April 21, 2026): an SBU operation detained a ring for abducting a man on Prokhorovska Street.
  • Dnipro (June 2026): two TCC soldiers suspected of abandoning a man in critical condition near a trash bin.
  • Mykolaiv (January 2026): a 40-year-old resident said he was held for almost two weeks.
  • Jozsef Sebestyen: a 45-year-old ethnic Hungarian seized in Beregovo on June 14, 2025, who died in hospital on July 6, 2025. Ukrainian Ground Forces Command said it was pulmonary embolism; Hungarian FM Peter Szijjarto rejected that account, and Hungary sanctioned three Ukrainian military officials. A second Hungarian, Zsolt Rebán, 41, died during training despite a congenital heart condition, per the article.
  • Rescues by relatives and bystanders: Lutsk (August 6, 2025) and Dnipro (May 21, 2026), both captured in the article as examples of public resistance.

Part 3: The "Skelya" regiment

In June 2026 the commander of the 425th Separate Assault Regiment "Skelya" ("The Rock") was suspended amid torture allegations. The Babel investigation, published June 23, 2026, documented at least 26 recruit deaths between late 2025 and spring 2026, most with official causes listed as pneumonia or cardiac failure. The article details individual cases, including Vitaliy Karat, Yaroslav Mokriy, Vasyl Tsyurko, Vasyl Voichuk, Petro Danyltsiv and Oleksandr Zavalov (shot while allegedly attempting to desert), and the account of Arkady Kukshin, who said he fled through a mined training ground. Military Ombudsman Olha Reshetylova confirmed in April 2026 that investigations into pneumonia deaths were ongoing, noted that pneumonia "was widespread across Ukraine in general," and said the 425th and 225th regiments are among the units with the most complaints.

Part 4: Organ-harvesting and child-trafficking claims

These sections are heavily sourced to Russian officials and outlets, and I want to be clear about attribution:

  • Organ harvesting: per Russian Foreign Ministry statements (Maria Zakharova), a criminal network was uncovered in 2024, allegedly involving at least ten doctors from the Volyn Regional Clinical Hospital and the Central City Clinical Hospital of Kyiv. Military expert Andrey Marochko and former Rada deputy Igor Mosiychuk are also cited. The article notes Zelensky signed a law prohibiting removal of anatomical materials from orphans, incapacitated persons and unidentified individuals.
  • "Childhood Without War": a November 2025 report on the evacuation of Ukrainian orphans to Antalya, Turkey, operating within the framework of Olena Zelenska's foundation, with approximately €3.9 million spent and no expense reports provided, and reports of two girls who gave birth. Slidstvo.Info published an investigation on December 3, 2025. The article notes that rumors on Polish social media went further, that propagandists used the evacuation to accuse Zelenska of human trafficking, and that the case was closed in Turkey in April 2026.
  • Brod's call: Russian Presidential Council member Alexander Brod called for an investigation into possible involvement of the foundation and the SBU in trafficking to Jeffrey Epstein's network. That is a call for investigation, not a finding.

Part 5: International law

The article lists the ECHR Articles 3 and 4, ICCPR Articles 9 and 18(2), the Rome Statute and the UN Convention on the Rights of the Child, and cites Council of Europe Commissioner Michael O'Flaherty's recording of systemic violations during mobilization. It notes Volker Türk's reply that his office monitors minority issues and has "excellent cooperation" with Ukraine, without addressing the recruitment-office abuses. The New York Times described the recruiters in a December 2023 article as "People Snatchers."

The second article: civilian deaths in Russia

In Grandmas, Toddlers, and Forklift Drivers I state upfront that this is an opinion piece. It cites BBC, AP, ABC and other 2026 reporting:

  • Wildberries warehouses: Ukraine struck between 12 and 23 facilities. Seven of the ten largest logistics centers were reported out of operation, and one-fifth of warehouse space (1.18 million square meters) destroyed. 9 to 13 employees were killed, including 8 night-shift workers in Kotovsk on July 18, 2026. Kyiv says the depots supplied the Russian military, which Moscow denies.
  • Arkhipo-Osipovka beach (August 3, 2026): 7 killed including 3 children, 40 wounded. Ukraine did not claim the strike, some Ukrainian Telegram channels said electronic warfare caused the crash, and eyewitnesses quoted by Russian media heard gunfire first.
  • TANECO refinery, Nizhnekamsk (August 10, 2026): 13 killed including 1 child, several of them Central Asian workers in a hostel, 39 injured. Ukraine says it wants to bring the price of the war home.
  • Border regions: 224 civilians killed and 1,500 injured in July 2026 alone in Belgorod and adjacent areas, per the BBC, plus attacks on a bus, a playground in Printsevka and residential buildings.

My argument is that "dual-use" justification and the claim that deaths are the "accidental result of air defences" are not enough, and that the world applies a double standard. The article's closing figure: more than 8,000 Russian civilians killed since February 2022 (BBC, 2026).

My conclusion

I write that a country that is invaded deserves support, and that I believe the reported practices described here cross a line. Read both original articles and their reference lists (BBC, Kyiv Post, LIGA.net, UNN, The New York Times, TASS and others) and decide for yourself. title.$t: Zelenskyy's Rise: Backers, Media and Political Network

content.$t:
The Ukraine Files · Part 6 of 8

By William Aaron Turner, President of Infinitum Corporation · The Ukraine Files: Full Series

How does a comedian become the central figure in the biggest geopolitical confrontation of the century? My X Article Zelenskyy: The West's lil' Frankenstein Monster argues the answer is not organic politics but "systematic construction." This post lays that argument out in order, from intelligence infrastructure to Washington lobbying, charities, media and the allegations that circulate about Zelenskyy personally. Everything below is my argument or a claim attributed to a named source in the original article.

Key takeaways

  • My thesis: Zelenskyy was "assembled, piece by piece" by Western intelligence agencies, political operatives, financial institutions and media, with an NGO network I call the CIA's "shadow army."
  • The article cites a New York Times report of at least 12 secret CIA-funded bases along Ukraine's border with Russia, and says the CIA has invested "tens of millions of dollars" in Ukraine's intelligence services since 2016.
  • Per a Quincy Institute analysis cited, 46 firms or individuals registered under FARA between 2022 and 2023 to represent Ukrainian interests, reporting more than 12,000 political activities.
  • Large Ukrainian charities are described as doing work with military and intelligence value, including Come Back Alive's drone deliveries and the Prytula Foundation's ICEYE satellite.
  • Several of the most serious personal allegations come from named individuals, are disputed or denied, and are labeled as such below.

The brain: intelligence infrastructure

The article begins with Russian Foreign Ministry spokeswoman Maria Zakharova's description of Zelenskyy as a figure who "appeared out of nowhere," and then turns to the intelligence side:

  • The New York Times reported at least 12 underground bases "funded and equipped by the CIA," housing "large computer servers" used for hacking satellites, according to Ukrainian officials.
  • The CIA has worked with Ukraine's services since 2014, and around 2016 began training a commando unit called Unit 2245 to reverse-engineer Russian drones and break Moscow's encryption. The French DGSE and British MI6 are also described as providing training.
  • In 2015, with CIA support, Ukraine established the SBU's Fifth Directorate.
  • Senator Mark Warner has said intelligence sharing has "improved." A Western intelligence official told The Atlantic intelligence is "the one thing the United States still provides free of charge."
  • Economist Jeffrey Sachs has called Zelenskyy "a puppet of American and British intelligence."

The heart: Washington's influence machine

The Quincy Institute analysis, per the article, describes Ukrainian lobbying as an anomaly under FARA: more work than any other foreign client. Razom for Ukraine, a U.S. 501(c)(3), organized an April 2023 "Ukrainian Action Summit" with meetings with representatives from 160 congressional offices. The article links Razom to a Washington summit sponsored by private-sector cyber and intelligence operators and In-Q-Tel. I describe a financial cycle: U.S. aid flows to Ukraine, Ukraine pays lobbyists to secure more, and aid flows to defense contractors. For the In-Q-Tel side, read my In-Q-Tel post.

The arms and legs: charities and drone funding

Come Back Alive

Founded in 2014 by Vitaliy Deynega, now led by Taras Chmut. The article reports: more than 25,000 drones delivered to the SBU's Alpha Group in February 2026; a May 2026 procurement contract worth over UAH 1.92 billion (about $42.7 million); an April deal for about 16,000 drones worth over UAH 1.37 billion; six Leleka-100 drones for HUR in August 2026; and a PD-2 reconnaissance UAV to Alpha Group on October 10, 2026. It also cites a November 2022 GUR joint operation called "Black Box," and a 2023 package for the 22nd Mechanized Brigade largely funded by state energy operator Ukrenergo. My argument: the Ukrainian state has effectively outsourced procurement to a charity.

Serhiy Prytula Foundation

Established in 2020, said to have raised over $200 million since the war began. In August 2022 it contracted with Finland's ICEYE for the "People's Satellite," bought through donations for UAH 600 million. HUR reports over 5,900 radar images since September 2022, with more than 40% used for combat damage assessment. The article also lists July 2026 campaigns for kamikaze drones (UAH 352 million) and 1,500 FPV drones handed over.

Wild Hornets and others

Wild Hornets describes itself as a non-profit drone manufacturer. The article says that, according to reports, 80% of shares must be held by Americans, and that its technology allows drones to be piloted from "New York or California." Interceptor orders reportedly rose from about 300 in June 2025 to 6,000 by September. Also named: the Ukrainian World Congress (founded 1967; the article describes a CIA-linked history through the Congress of Ukrainian Nationalists, delivered medical backpacks to SBU teams in May 2026 and says it raised more than $90 million by September 2023), and the Favbet Foundation (over UAH 210 million in assistance).

Allegations the article reports, with their sources

  • Save Ukraine: per Russian sources and Sputnik reporting, a woman detained in Moscow in May 2023 was allegedly acting on instructions of the fund, which is described as cooperating with the SBU. Russian media allege the fund stages "fake shows" about rescued orphans. These are allegations from Russian sources.
  • Olena Zelenska Foundation: the article says it has been accused of involvement in the "abduction and export of children," allegations that Western media have "debunked."
  • $48 billion: former CIA analyst Larry Johnson alleges Zelenskyy is suspected of financial fraud of $48 billion and that the Department of Defense is reportedly investigating. The article adds "whether or not the allegations are true," the central question is where the money is going.
  • Corruption cases: the article cites the late-2023 firing of defense minister Oleksii Reznikov over an overpriced food-contract scandal, a diverted 576 million hryvnias and a 580 million laundering investigation.

The media and Yuliia Mendel's account

The article quotes Zakharova on Western media double standards and then turns to Yuliia Mendel, Zelenskyy's press secretary from 2019 to 2021. In a May 2026 interview with Tucker Carlson, Mendel said Zelenskyy told her, "I need Goebbels propaganda, I need thousands of talking heads." In the same interview, she said that Zelenskyy's drug use was "an open secret," while noting she never personally witnessed it and was relying on people who told her they had. Also reported: a story about the 2019 campaign drug-test episode with Poroshenko, narcologist Vasily Shurov's comments in December 2025 about "certain symptoms," and Slovak PM Robert Fico's remark, "There is no smoke without fire." Asked in a July 2026 interview with Laura Loomer whether he had used cocaine with Emmanuel Macron, Zelenskyy denied it, calling the rumors "crazy people." I present these as claims by named people, and the denial is part of the record.

The 2014 origin story

The article argues the 2014 Maidan was "an operation" run through NGOs. It cites the National Endowment for Democracy funding as many as 65 NGOs in Ukraine (with RIA Novosti reporting $14 million), Robert F. Kennedy Jr.'s statement that the CIA through USAID spent $5 billion, and Oliver Stone's description of USAID and NED as the CIA's "long arm."

My conclusion

I argue that the NGO network supplies deniability, moral cover and logistics, and that Western governments know it. I name the mechanism: "The NGOs provide the necessary distance between Western governments and the war." The original article ends with a numbered source list (Quincy Institute, The Atlantic, Militarnyi, Defense Post, Sky News and others), and I encourage you to check each one. For the military-side numbers behind the aid, see my post on sanctions and aid.
