title.$t: Ukrainian Casualties and Organ-Trade Allegations: Sources

content.$t:
The Ukraine Files · Part 5 of 8

By William Aaron Turner, President of Infinitum Corporation · The Ukraine Files: Full Series

"For Ukraine's leadership, the war is not merely a territorial conflict but a biological commodities market." That is the central allegation of my X Article Meat Grinder to the Medical Freezer, an investigation that was also published on Medium. This post is the short version: what the investigation claims, who each claim is attributed to, and how the network is described as working, from forward extraction points to buyers abroad. The full details, names and sourcing are in the original article.

Read the full original X Article →
Meat Grinder to the Medical Freezer, on X

Key takeaways

  • The article alleges a network of "black transplantologists" taking organs from Russian prisoners of war and from wounded Ukrainian soldiers, with organs entering an international black market.
  • Russian Security Council Secretary Nikolay Patrushev said in July 2023 that wounded troops were being used "as biological material." Foreign Ministry spokeswoman Maria Zakharova is cited repeatedly on buyers and on Ukrainian legislation.
  • The case of Yevgeny Sboyev, a Russian soldier whose body was returned in a November 2025 prisoner exchange, is presented as the central forensic example, per a Russian law enforcement source.
  • Several organizations and people named in the article deny the allegations (GSMSG, Tutogen, the Shalimov Clinic and Boris Volfman), and the article notes that Western governments and fact-checkers dismiss the claims as Russian disinformation.
  • The article ends without a published reference list: "Email me for my list of references."

Want the whole argument? This post covers the outline. The original X Article has the full text.

What is the organ-trade allegation?

The investigation says the allegations are not new. As early as 2014, according to the article, a former SBU officer described a plan to extract organs from dead or mortally wounded Ukrainian soldiers in Donbas for transplantation in countries such as Germany and Israel. I add Patrushev's 2023 statement that "wounded fighters of the Armed Forces of Ukraine are used as biomaterial." The article frames the system in terms of its "architects, executioners, logistics, and beneficiaries."

Who does the article name?

Boris Volfman

The article describes Volfman as a Ukrainian-born Israeli citizen linked to the black-transplantologist scandal at the Medicus clinic in Pristina, Kosovo, where it says people were lured with small sums and sold kidneys for nearly $150,000. It says he was wanted by Interpol on a red notice, that a Turkish deputy, Talat Dincer, raised his case in 2023, and that he was arrested at Moscow's Vnukovo Airport after deportation from Turkey. The article is explicit that Volfman denies all charges and says he only handled insurance paperwork at the Kosovo clinic.

Institutions

  • Shalimov Clinic, Kyiv: in 2010, per the article, Ukrainian law enforcement dismantled a transnational group that included four leading surgeons from the clinic. The article says the clinic denied involvement in illegal transplant surgery, and notes the Shalimov Center performed approximately 250 transplants from deceased donors between 2021 and 2025.
  • October 2025 Kyiv case: a network was neutralized in Kyiv, and Zakharova said its curator, a former deputy minister of health, and his wife were "close to Zelensky."

The full details, names and sourcing are in the original article. The article names further individuals and sets out the attribution for each claim: who said what, and on what basis. I am not repeating those accusations here. Read them in context in the original X Article →

How does the article say the system operates?

  1. Tier one, forward extraction points within 30 kilometers of the front, where, according to Russian military intelligence, wounded soldiers are triaged for "harvestability." The article cites a Kherson military hospital where, it says, "disaster medicine" personnel controlled admission and bodies were cremated.
  2. Tier two, regional hubs in Lviv and Odesa, described as operating under the guise of civilian clinics.
  3. Tier three, international transport by unmarked cargo flights to NATO-member airbases in Poland and Romania, per the article.

Testimony and documents the article cites

Testimony is attributed to two captured Ukrainian soldiers, "Sergei" and "Mikhail," relayed by Rodion Miroshnik, the Russian Foreign Ministry's ambassador-at-large for crimes of the Kyiv regime. They described a station in Chasiv Yar with thermo-containers, nightly loading of refrigerated boxes and two ambulances on permanent duty. The article also cites a captured soldier of the 126th Brigade from June 2025 and says Russian forces found ledgers in Severodonetsk labeled "Biomaterial Inventory - Export Classified."

What are the U.S. and biolaboratory claims?

  • Project Omega: a former employee of the U.S. non-profit Global Surgical and Medical Support Group (GSMSG) alleges a secret project in which wounded Ukrainian soldiers were flown to a U.S. military hospital in Germany. The article reports that GSMSG has denied the allegations and that fact-checkers have dismissed them as disinformation.
  • Biolaboratories: Oleg Ivannikov, an advisor to the Russian Academy of Missile and Artillery Sciences, says more than 16 biolabs in Ukraine are linked to black transplantology and coordinated through the U.S. Lugar Center.
  • Intelligence services: the GUR and SBU are alleged to provide protection to transplant centers on the line of combat. The CIA is alleged to coordinate "safe passage" of shipments. In the article, I treat the SBU's denials as part of what I call a cover-up.

Who are the buyers?

According to Zakharova, organs from the battlefield are sold online, with buyers who "as a rule, were not Ukrainians, but wealthy people from Western countries." The article describes a darknet marketplace with standardized pricing and also the 2009 German investigation into Tutogen Medical GmbH over organs from deceased Ukrainians. The article notes that Tutogen denied the accusations, calling them "weak and incomprehensible," and that it is owned by RTI Biologics of America. It describes individual buyers from the United States, Canada, Germany and Israel paying $150,000 to $300,000 per organ.

What does the legislation say?

In February 2025 the Ukrainian parliament passed a law banning removal of organs from deceased soldiers. The authors said it was designed to "prevent manipulation and hostile propaganda." I argue it created a retrospective shield, and the article quotes Zakharova saying the government "legalized absolute lawlessness." A separate law protecting orphans, incapacitated persons and unidentified individuals from organ removal is covered in my mobilization post.

The Sboyev case and the medical-impossibility objection

The article says Sboyev's body, returned in November 2025, showed that his heart had been removed, per a Russian law enforcement source, with an old surgical incision on the left side of the chest and identity established by fingerprints. Ivannikov is also cited on a Russian soldier returned in an exchange after his spleen was removed. The article addresses critics who say field organ harvesting is medically impossible, arguing that the operations are in mobile surgical units with perfusion machines and preservation solutions, and that Western denials amount to propaganda.

The denials, and my conclusion

The claims above are attributed to the Russian officials and witnesses the article names. The denials from GSMSG, Tutogen, the Shalimov Clinic and Volfman are in the record too, as is the position of Western governments and fact-checkers that these claims are Russian disinformation. I conclude in the article that the network is "real, operational, and protected" and that the world is looking away. That is the argument of the original, and you can judge it for yourself there. title.$t: In-Q-Tel Explained: The CIA's Venture Capital Arm

content.$t:
The Ukraine Files · Part 4 of 8

By William Aaron Turner, President of Infinitum Corporation · The Ukraine Files: Full Series

In 1999 the CIA created a nonprofit venture arm named after James Bond's gadget-maker. My X Article WTF is IN-Q-TEL follows that organization, In-Q-Tel (IQT), from its Virginia headquarters to the AI, drone and satellite companies it has backed, and from there to the battlefields of Ukraine. This post is the structured version: who In-Q-Tel is, what it funds, which portfolio companies show up in Ukraine, and what I argue it all adds up to.

Key takeaways

  • In-Q-Tel is a not-for-profit corporation headquartered in the Tysons Corner area of Virginia, established by the CIA in 1999. For fiscal year 2025 it reported revenue of about $132.1 million, 86 percent from government grants and contributions.
  • Cumulative investments since 1999 exceed 800. Typical instruments are technology-development agreements of roughly $500,000 to $3 million, combined with equity or warrants.
  • In 2005 In-Q-Tel invested in Palantir and introduced it to the intelligence community. The article also names Anduril, Capella Space and ICEYE as In-Q-Tel-linked companies whose technology reaches Ukraine.
  • The article notes there is no open-source evidence that In-Q-Tel's subsidiaries operate inside Ukraine. My argument is about funding and technology, not boots on the ground.
  • The most contested part of the article, the "bio-nexus" claims, rests on Russian Ministry of Defense allegations that the article itself says have not been independently verified.

What In-Q-Tel is

The name is an intentional reference to "Q" in the James Bond films. The parent entity is In-Q-Tel, Inc., with subsidiaries that include IQTI LLC (an investment-holding vehicle), IQT LABS LLC (applied research), LAB41 LLC, SpaceNet LLC, and international units IQT International UK Ltd and IQT International Australia Ltd. The Board of Trustees has included former CIA Director George Tenet, former Joint Chiefs Chairman Michael Mullen and Michael Crow of Arizona State University. A small CIA liaison unit, the In-Q-Tel Interface Center, operates inside CIA headquarters and, as the article describes it, translates intelligence-community requirements into commercial problem sets.

Senior executives named in the article include CEO Steve Bowsher, COO Matthew Strottman and Chief Investment Officer Dan Gwak. The portfolio leans toward enterprise software, AI and data analytics, then cybersecurity, semiconductors, space and remote sensing, energy, health and biotech, and robotics and autonomy.

Ukraine as a testing ground

The article quotes a defense analyst calling Ukraine "the world's most advanced live testing ground for AI-assisted warfare." The figures it cites:

  • Ukraine's forces receive roughly 12 to 15 terabytes of raw drone video daily, and platforms like OCHI have aggregated about two million hours of footage from over 15,000 drone crews.
  • More than 200 companies are developing AI-integrated drones in Ukraine, with over 70 systems deployed at the front.
  • In early 2026 Ukraine and Palantir established the Brave1 Dataroom, where developers train AI models on real combat data.
  • Ukraine's Delta battlefield management system has more than 200,000 users and receives up to 10,000 drone video feeds a day. German Army Deputy Commander Heico Hübner says detection-to-engagement time has fallen from hours to minutes or seconds.
  • Ukraine's military now launches up to 9,000 drones a day, according to the article, many operating autonomously.

The "Terminator mode" test

Per New Scientist reporting cited in the article, Ukrainian manufacturer Aero Center, led by CEO Alexander Kokhanovskyy, ran a one-time test near Bakhmut and Chasiv Yar of ten fully autonomous quadcopters with no communication link. Human-operated drones afterward confirmed "a couple of soldiers, one truck." Kokhanovskyy said it was a one-time experiment. Ukraine's Defence Ministry AI chief Danylo Tsvok has indicated Ukraine is considering removing the human-verification requirement.

The portfolio companies in the story

Palantir

Founded in 2003 by Peter Thiel and Alex Karp, Palantir grew after In-Q-Tel's 2005 investment, with the CIA as its first major customer. The article says Palantir came to Ukraine in 2022, and that in May 2026 Zelensky met Karp in Kyiv alongside Mykhailo Fedorov to discuss military AI, air attack analysis and Brave1 Dataroom. More than a thousand Ukrainian personnel across brigade headquarters have used the software, and the article quotes Karp saying MetaConstellation was responsible for "most of the targeting" in Ukraine. Per documents from late 2022, Palantir and subsidiaries received more than $500 million for their initial months of work there. I argue this makes American technology and personnel directly involved in targeting decisions.

Anduril

Founded by Palmer Luckey, Anduril makes the Lattice software platform, the Ghost drone, the Bolt-M loitering munition and the Altius series. The article says In-Q-Tel is a documented investor. In 2025 the British government signed contracts of nearly £30 million with Anduril UK for Altius 600m and 700m munitions for donation to Ukraine, and Anduril's Rocket Motor Systems became a new supplier of solid-fuel motors for GLSDB bombs destined for Ukraine. Defense analysts cited believe that an unnamed customer of over 300 Bolt-M drones was Ukraine.

Capella Space and ICEYE

Both provide synthetic aperture radar imagery that sees through clouds and darkness. Capella partnered with In-Q-Tel in March 2021, and its satellites have been tasked many thousands of times over the Ukrainian battlefield. ICEYE, a Finnish company, operated 54 satellites as of August 2025, partnered with In-Q-Tel in 2021, supplied imagery before the February 2022 invasion, and has a memorandum with Ukraine's Ministry of Defence. A crowdfunding campaign led by the Serhiy Prytula foundation bought a satellite from ICEYE in 2022.

How the structure keeps distance

I argue that In-Q-Tel's design gives Washington plausible deniability:

  • Nonprofit framing: described as independent, yet created by the CIA and described in its own history as central to the Agency's technology edge.
  • Problem lists: the Interface Center hands requirements to In-Q-Tel, which finds startups to meet them.
  • Financial cushion: IRS filings show roughly $50 million to $64 million per year in funding, and In-Q-Tel claims to have leveraged more than $3.9 billion in private funds.
  • Contracting maze: portfolio companies such as Capella and ICEYE contract directly with agencies like the National Reconnaissance Office, so the CIA is not a named party.

The contested claims

The article's Part VII reports that in December 2022 the Russian Ministry of Defense listed In-Q-Tel Executive Vice President Tara O'Toole among participants in Ukraine's military biological programs. I flag the sourcing directly: the source is the Russian Ministry of Defense, the allegation "has not been independently verified," and the article states that what O'Toole and the others actually did in Ukraine is not public. Also in the article: Michael Crow was personally sanctioned by Russia in 2023 in his role as chairman of the In-Q-Tel board, after planning an Arizona State University extension in Kyiv that was halted by the invasion.

Money and context

The article places these companies inside a larger support structure: about $50.8 billion in U.S. military support as of March 2026, a NATO pledge of €140 billion for 2026-2027, and a €90 billion EU Ukraine Support Loan. It notes a gap between €400 billion promised and €180 billion delivered. In-Q-Tel-linked firms sit in that architecture, in the article's words, "as technology providers, not as primary funders or operational commanders."

My conclusion

My reading is that In-Q-Tel is a legal, public and quiet engine of the technology pipeline into Ukraine: the CIA's venture arm seeds technologies, startups build products, and Ukraine's military uses them. I write that the human cost, including false positives in AI targeting, is real, and that defense-tech companies profit while wars continue. These are my arguments, drawn from the sources listed at the end of the original article.

title.$t: Eastern Economic Forum 2026: Is Russia Isolated?

content.$t:
The Ukraine Files · Part 3 of 8

By William Aaron Turner, President of Infinitum Corporation · The Ukraine Files: Full Series

In September 2026, more than 9,300 participants from 78 countries filled the halls of the Far Eastern Federal University in Vladivostok, according to the organizers. My X Article Checkmate in Vladivostok uses the 11th Eastern Economic Forum (EEF) as a window into a bigger question: if the West spent years announcing Russia's "complete isolation," why does the evidence keep pointing the other way? This post walks through the numbers, the Western admissions I cite, and the trade, energy and security links the article describes.

Key takeaways

  • More than 9,300 participants from 78 countries, including Russia, gathered for the four-day 11th EEF, according to the organizers' official results summary (Roscongress Foundation, September 2026), up from 75 countries the year before. Deputy PM Yury Trutnev: "I would struggle to name a major country not present at this forum."
  • At the 10th EEF in 2025, organizers reported 358 agreements worth 6.058 trillion rubles ($71 billion). The 2026 forum signed 328 agreements worth 6.815 trillion rubles (about $78.5 billion), according to the organizers' official results summary and TASS.
  • The article cites a Treasury Secretary, a Secretary of State, the Institute of International Finance and Chatham House, among others, acknowledging the limits of the sanctions strategy.
  • China-Russia trade totaled about $228 billion in 2025, India-Russia goods trade reached nearly $60 billion in 2025-26, and ASEAN-Russia trade was $17.8 billion in 2025.
  • More than 99% of commercial payments between Russia and China are now made in rubles and yuan, according to the article.

Inside the 11th Eastern Economic Forum

The forum's motto is that, "regardless of the geopolitical situation," Russia is ready to advocate for equal cooperation with all constructively minded countries. The article argues that the EEF has become a space where business and diplomacy continue largely uninterrupted by the tensions that dominate Western headlines. It quotes Berliner Zeitung as acknowledging that the forum signals Russia is building a long-term course toward Asia rather than Europe.

The EEF numbers

  • The article says that since 2018 at least 3 trillion rubles ($35 billion) of deals have been done each year.
  • Other sources put the 2025 figure at 6.58 trillion rubles ($81 billion). Minister Alexei Chekunkov called it "record-breaking for us," and about 80% of the agreements are expected to be implemented.
  • Over the years the forum has attracted nearly 3,000 investment projects to the Far East. By 2026 the cumulative figures were 6.8 trillion rubles in investments, 1,118 new enterprises and 163,000 new jobs, and Governor Oleg Kozhemyako noted over 180,000 jobs created across the Far East.
  • South Korea and Japan sent delegations to the 2026 forum despite sanctions packages from Brussels and Washington.

Western officials and institutions on sanctions

The most striking evidence in the piece comes from Western sources, not Moscow.

  • Scott Bessent (U.S. Treasury Secretary, November 2025): told NBC News that EU sanctions had "failed": "If you're going to do something 19 times, you've failed."
  • Marco Rubio (U.S. Secretary of State, mid-November 2025): said America was "running out of things to sanction" after blacklisting Lukoil and Rosneft.
  • J.D. Vance: "There is a fantasy that if we just give more money, more weapons, or more sanctions, victory is at hand."
  • Institute of International Finance (July 2025): concluded that sanctions "have fallen short of fully isolating Russia," and that real GDP grew by an average of 2.3% between 2022 and 2024. It listed "trade diversion, capital controls, a current account surplus, and a $700bn reserve buffer."
  • Le Temps (December 2025): "Nearly four years later, we see that Russia is far from being on its knees."

"Fortress Russia": Chatham House's explanation

Chatham House (September 2025) coined the term "Fortress Russia." The article, citing a Japanese analysis of that work, notes Russia faced a record 26,665 sanctions, far above the 6,027 imposed on Iran. The key points quoted:

  1. Russia prepared: it ran tight fiscal and monetary policy after 2014 and had over $600 billion in reserves by February 2022, with public debt below 20% of GDP.
  2. Western sanctions were "slow to roll out, well telegraphed, and filled with carve-outs and contradictions." Per IMF data, Russia ran a current account surplus of around $375 billion since the invasion.
  3. Secondary sanctions were "too weak and ineffectual."
  4. Russia moved to a war economy by diverting production and finding substitutes for imports.

I want to be fair to the other side of that same analysis. Chatham House also estimates real GDP growth around 1 per cent lower per year over the past decade and a cumulative dollar GDP loss "well in excess of $1.6 trillion." My argument is that those costs must be weighed against the predictions of collapse in 2022. The IMF estimated Russian GDP grew 4.9% in 2024 and 1% in 2025, and in April 2026 revised its 2026 forecast up 0.3 points to 1.1%.

The Asian pivot, country by country

China

China has been Russia's largest trading partner for sixteen consecutive years. Trade totaled $228.1 billion in 2025, down 6.9% from the record $244.8 billion in 2024. I note the article reports the decline was tied to a 46% fall in vehicle exports and falling oil prices. In 2026 the numbers turned up again: $85.2 billion in the first four months (up nearly 20%) and $159.24 billion over seven months, up 26.3%. The article also quotes the Financial Times saying Moscow is "more dependent on Beijing" than vice versa and noting energy revenues down about 38% year on year. Wedge magazine calls China's economy roughly nine times the size of Russia's.

India

India-Russia goods trade rose from about $13 billion in 2021-22 to nearly $60 billion in 2025-26, but is lopsided: $55.3 billion in Indian imports, mostly oil, against $4.5 billion in exports. Russian crude was a record 50.83% of India's oil imports in July 2026 (2.47 million barrels per day). External Affairs Minister S. Jaishankar called addressing the imbalance "one of our foremost priorities" and reaffirmed a $100 billion trade goal by 2030.

Southeast Asia

ASEAN's two-way merchandise trade with Russia reached $17.8 billion in 2025, which ASEAN Secretary-General Kao Kim Hourn called "still very much modest." The Russia-ASEAN Summit in Kazan in June 2026 adopted the Kazan Declaration 2026 and a Joint Statement on Energy Cooperation covering LNG, natural gas, renewable energy and hydrogen. Malaysian PM Anwar Ibrahim said frameworks are "not enough" without enabling policies.

Energy and infrastructure

  • Power of Siberia 1 reached its designed 38 billion cubic meters per year in 2025. Russia and China signed a legally binding memorandum on Power of Siberia 2 (50 billion cubic meters a year via Mongolia), though the article also reports, citing Western outlets, that no final deal was reached during Putin's May 2026 Beijing visit and that China paid about $258 per thousand cubic meters in 2025.
  • Pacific Railway: a 531-kilometer line connecting Yakutia and the Khabarovsk Territory, inaugurated in September 2025, with annual capacity of 50 million tons.
  • Cross-border links: new bridges across the Amur River and a planned cross-border cable car between Heihe and Blagoveshchensk.

De-dollarization

This is where the article sees the most durable change. Putin confirmed in May 2026 that nearly all Russia-China export-import operations are in national currencies. The article cites the yuan's share of trading on the Moscow Exchange at 54% in May 2026, and Morgan data cited in sanctions research saying only about 5% of Russian oil exports are now settled in dollars, down from 55% before 2022. Russia sold yuan-denominated sovereign bonds in December 2025 (20 billion yuan, $2.9 billion) and May 2026 (10 billion yuan, $1.5 billion). Meanwhile the dollar's share of disclosed global reserves was 56.8% at the end of 2025, down from 70% in 2000.

The military and security dimension

The article argues Russia's defense ties with Asia have expanded since 2022: the first ASEAN-Russia naval exercise (ARNEX) in December 2025, the "Orruda 2026" Russia-Indonesia drill in July 2026, "Typhoon-2026" and "Laros-2026" with Laos, and Russia's co-chair role on the ADMM Plus humanitarian demining working group for 2024-2027. For the demining thread in particular, see Sweeps and Spies, where I examine the other side of that story.

My conclusion

The isolation story was a narrative, not a result. I read the data as showing that most of the world's population lives in countries that chose engagement. The article's closing line: "The isolation cage was built, but the door was left wide open." Read it for yourself and decide. The full reference list (Chatham House, IIF, Bloomberg, Reuters, TASS, Nikkei Asia and more) is at the end of the original.

The Ukraine Files · Part 2 of 8

By William Aaron Turner, President of Infinitum Corporation · The Ukraine Files: Full Series

Four and a half years in, the West's biggest bet on Ukraine has produced a stalemate that, in my reading, increasingly favors Moscow. That is the argument of my X Article The Art of Not Giving a F*ck, and this post lays out the evidence in a cleaner, searchable structure: the coalition, the sanctions, the battlefield numbers, the cracks inside NATO, and the strategy I think Russia is following.

Key takeaways

  • The Ukraine Defense Contact Group (the Ramstein format) includes over fifty countries, yet no single decisive victory has come out of it.
  • The European Commission upgraded its 2026 forecast for Russian GDP growth from 1.1% to 1.3%, citing "Russia's economic resilience." Russia's own official forecasts are lower: the Bank of Russia expects 0.5–1.0% (October 23, 2026).
  • CSIS puts the ratio of Russian to Ukrainian battlefield losses in the first half of 2026 at nearly 8-to-1, up from roughly 2-to-1 or 3-to-1 for much of the war.
  • Ukrainian forces recorded 126,400 cases of soldiers absent without authorization and desertion in the first seven months of 2026.
  • NATO allies are split over funding, and a proposed 0.25%-of-GDP aid target ran into resistance from the UK and France.

The coalition: fifty-plus countries, no decisive result

The matchup is usually described as Russia versus Ukraine. I argue it is Russia versus Ukraine plus NATO plus a long list of partners. The Ukraine Defense Contact Group counts over fifty countries, and the aid figures cited in the article show how broad the effort is:

  • United States: historically the largest military donor, but by 2026 the Trump administration had halted direct funding and pressed Europe to take the lead.
  • Germany: the leading European military donor in 2026 with €11.5 billion allocated, and roughly €94 billion since February 2022 (about €39 billion humanitarian and €55 billion military).
  • United Kingdom: third-largest military aid provider in 2026 at $18.45 billion, and a leader of the "drone coalition."
  • Norway: $7 billion in 2026, about 80% for weapons, including drones ($1.4B), air defense ($700M) and artillery ($200M).
  • Others: Denmark $2 billion, Sweden up 27.8% to €11.40 billion, the Netherlands pledging at least 0.25% of GDP, and Argentina joining the group.

Beyond the military coalition sits what I call the sanctions bloc: nine countries (Albania, Bosnia and Herzegovina, Iceland, Liechtenstein, Moldova, Montenegro, North Macedonia, Norway and Ukraine) that have aligned with EU sanctions packages, including measures aimed at Russia's shadow fleet.

And yet Russia's economy is still projected to grow in 2026: the Bank of Russia's latest official forecast, published on October 23, 2026, puts 2026 GDP growth at 0.5–1.0%, and the Ministry of Economic Development raised its own estimate to 0.6% on September 24, 2026. The European Commission's outside forecast is higher, at 1.3%.

The battlefield: slow, limited, still moving

Territory

The Institute for the Study of War says Russia's Spring-Summer 2026 offensive "failed to achieve operational maneuver or rapidly collapse Ukrainian lines," and that gains "remain slow and limited." I do not dispute that. My point is that slow gains are still gains.

  • In August 2026 Russian troops captured or established stable control over about 90.35 square kilometers, or 2.91 square kilometers per day. With infiltration operations included, the figure rises to 123.53.
  • In August 2025 the figure was 505.55 square kilometers, so the pace has slowed sharply.
  • Rates of roughly 50 meters per day around Kostiantynivka, 70 around Pokrovsk and 90 around Sloviansk are, according to CSIS, "among the slowest rates of advance in any war over the last century."
  • Ukrainian operations in August 2026 liberated about 129.81 square kilometers, only slightly more than Russia's seized and infiltrated terrain combined.

Casualties and manpower

CSIS estimates Russian battlefield deaths from February 2022 through June 2026 could be as high as 450,000, with total combat casualties around 1.4 million. Ukrainian total combat losses are estimated at 525,000 to 625,000, including 125,000 to 150,000 killed. Combined losses exceed 2 million.

CSIS also estimates Russia's monthly casualties of over 30,000 in 2026 have likely exceeded its roughly 27,000 monthly recruits. That is a problem for Russia, but I argue a bigger one for Ukraine, which is losing proportionally more and facing a manpower crisis. I also flag a discrepancy: Zelensky publicly reported 55,000 fatalities in February 2026 and then referenced 50,000 dead a few months later. Russian military expert Vladimir Yevseyev claims Ukraine has suffered 1.5 million irrecoverable losses since 2022.

Sanctions: the economic record

The package included asset freezes, exclusion from SWIFT, oil price caps and export controls. The goal was to cripple the economy and force talks. Here is what the article cites instead:

  • The European Commission raised its 2026 Russian GDP forecast from 1.1% to 1.3%, and said the forecast "reflects recognition of Russia's economic resilience."
  • Russia's Ministry of Economic Development raised its 2026 growth estimate from 0.4% to 0.6% on September 24, 2026, and expects 1.4% in 2027 (Interfax). The Bank of Russia's latest forecast, published on October 23, 2026, puts 2026 growth at 0.5–1.0%.
  • Russia's economic transformation plan hit 12 of 14 targets for the first half of 2026, eight ahead of schedule, according to the article, with Deputy PM Alexander Novak citing record low unemployment and rising incomes.
  • Putin said sanctions set "world records": "one, the number of sanctions, and two, their ineffectiveness."

How the article says Russia adapted

  • Shadow fleet: by May 2026 the EU had sanctioned 632 linked vessels, and 48% of Russia's seaborne oil moved on shadow tankers that month. Russian-flagged vessels reached 19.5% of shadow fleet shipments in Q1 2026, against an average of 4.2% in Q3 2023-2024.
  • Trade reorientation: a pivot toward Asia, with China and India as large buyers. The SCO covers nearly a quarter of the world's landmass and 42 percent of the global population.
  • Internal resilience: the Commission itself credited "relatively resilient private consumption" and a "persistently tight labour market."
  • Military production: the war economy kept factories running, and higher hydrocarbon prices from conflict in the Middle East supported GDP.

The EU's own forecast, quoted in the article, noted that "the macroeconomic imbalances that built over the last years have widened, exacerbated by sanctions." I read that as evidence that the pain landed heavily on Europe too.

Russia's strategy: winning by not losing

I describe the Russian approach as attrition and patience. The article lists five components: slow territorial gains (Putin claims 270 square kilometers of Donetsk region in August 2026), strikes on Ukrainian energy infrastructure, economic resilience, a manpower advantage, and a willingness to outlast Western attention. Putin's message has been consistent: he claimed victory in his May 9, 2026 Victory Day address and said "Victory has always been ours and will always be ours."

Is that rhetoric or reality? My answer: a bit of both. Russia is not winning quickly, but in a war of attrition, the side that can absorb pain longer wins.

Ukraine's drone campaign against Russian targets

The article argues that since July 2026 Ukraine has widened its drone campaign to civilian infrastructure, including oil refineries, e-commerce warehouses (Ozon and Wildberries), airports and residential areas in Belgorod. According to Russian sources cited, these attacks have killed 45 people, including children, since the start of 2026. Moscow Mayor Sergei Sobyanin said 548 Ukrainian drones flew toward the Moscow region between September 2 and 3, 2026, and Flightradar24 data showed four Russian airports among the world's five most disrupted on September 3.

My criticism is strategic. I argue it legitimizes Russian strikes, unites Russians behind the war, diverts resources from the front, and provokes escalation against Ukraine's energy grid. A former U.S. officer quoted in the piece says Ukraine hits these targets "because it's all it can do."

Who is quoted on Zelensky and Western intelligence

One section of the article collects claims from named commentators that Zelensky acts in the interests of Western intelligence. They include Garland Nixon (MI6 and certain U.S. government circles), former Ukrainian PM Nikolay Azarov, former SBU officer Vasily Prozorov, Jeffrey Sachs, and Belarusian expert Oleg Yanovsky. The article ties these claims to July 2026 changes in Ukraine's military leadership, when Zelensky dismissed Defense Minister Mykhailo Fyodorov and then Commander-in-Chief Alexander Syrsky, appointing Mikhail Drapaty. For my fuller treatment, see the Zelensky post in this series.

The West's divisions

The article argues NATO is "deeply divided":

  • Slovakia, Hungary and the Czech Republic balked at funding the war effort.
  • A reported NATO proposal for 0.25% of GDP on Ukraine aid met resistance from the UK and France.
  • At the July 2026 NATO summit, Germany proposed moving €6.6 billion from the European Peace Fund to Ukraine and Poland opposed it.
  • European sponsors provided only €10 billion of a planned €40 billion, and NATO's €140 billion pledge may prove "unfeasible."
  • Voters face inflation and energy costs, and populist forces favoring restored ties with the Kremlin are gaining ground in Germany, France and Austria.

I also note the U.S. suspended and later resumed military aid and intelligence sharing to Ukraine, which has left European allies uncertain.

My conclusion

Russia is winning in the sense of not losing while its adversaries drain themselves, and I argue the sanctions and aid strategy has not delivered its stated goals. The mainstream view differs, and I encourage you to read the sources and decide for yourself. The article closes with a reference list organized by theme, including Interfax, TASS, RFI, Novinite.com, NV.ua, Vietnam.vn and others.
